English.Text: It is time for the evening tales, to teach the young ones virtue and piety, but I... seem to have forgotten some parts of the story.
The Envoy needs your help piecing together an instructive tale for the children's story hour. Much to his vexation, he appears to have forgotten many of its most important parts.
The Envoy needs your help remembering parts of a tale he wants to tell the children.

Once upon a time, long, long ago, a sultan had only one son, renowned for being kind and compassionate to all.
One day, as he was exploring his father's lands, he came upon a young Bedouin girl struggling to draw water from a desert well. Now the prince was... err...
Very clever, so he tied a stone to the end of the rope to make the pulling easier.
Tall and strong! He pulled on the rope and... whoosh! Up came the bucket!

The bucket came easily out of the well, and the girl thanked the prince by giving him a pouch of her sweetest dates.
Delighted, the prince thanked her and went on his way, until he reached the edge of his father's lands. He had walked for hours and was very hungry, and he was just opening the pouch of dates when a lion leapt out in front of him! So the prince...
Shared his dates with the lion.
Smeared himself with sticky date syrup to put the lion off.

The lion's jaw fell open in surprise! "I have never met a human who was not afraid of me— much less one willing to share his meal with me!"
The prince replied: "We should always show a kind heart. Everyone deserves compassion, be they camel, human or lion."
Impressed by these wise words, the lion followed the prince back to his father's palace. The prince became a beloved sultan, and he and the lion remained the best of friends for as long as they lived. And that is why, to this day, a lion guards the gates of the palace.

"Eat me now and the syrup will glue your jaws shut!" exclaimed the prince. The lion sighed: "Then I shall wait for it to dry, and eat you afterwards."
"Fair enough," said the prince, "but in the meantime, tell me: what is it like to be a lion?"
They talked for so long that by the time the syrup had dried, the lion no longer wished to eat the prince at all. The prince offered the lion a place at his side, and that is why, to this day, a lion guards the gates of the palace.

In a matter of minutes, the prince had drawn enough water for the girl's whole family. He helped her carry it to their tent, where he met her father, a poor old man who had little to offer by way of thanks but insisted that the prince stay the night. Exhausted, the prince gladly accepted.
In the middle of the night, however, the prince was woken by a low hissing. Still half asleep, he sat up to ask for some quiet— and froze when he saw two enormous pale snakes beside his bed.
Despite the danger, the prince kept his composure and... hmm...
Struck at both snakes at once.
Politely asked the snakes to be a little quieter.

Seizing the sword by his pillow, the prince struck out and slew both snakes with a single blow! But as they fell to the ground, their bodies shimmered and changed, revealing two very young, very dead men. Woken by the noise, the old man hobbled into the tent and began to weep. "My boys! What have you done? You seemed so kind-hearted, I thought you would break the djinn's curse— but now... how could you!"
Red-faced with shame and remorse, the prince fled back to his father's palace, swearing before Allah never again to judge by appearances, and to be good to all, human or otherwise.

"You... you do not fear us?" the astonished snakes asked.
"Why should I?" answered the prince. "We are all Allah's creatures, and you deserve as much respect as any other."
At these words, the snakes' skin shimmered and blurred, and soon two young boys stood in their place. "Father, father!" one of them cried with joy. The old man rushed into the tent and wept to see his sons. "I knew it! Only one as wise as you could treat them kindly and break the djinn's curse! A thousand blessings upon a prince with such kindness in his heart!"
Soon the tale of the prince's wisdom spread through all the land, and everyone praised him and strove, like him, not to judge others so hastily.
